text: Time to put the whole chapter together into one real, working build. The scenario: Incident doesn't stand alone on the platform — it actually extends the Task table, inheriting fields like short_description, assigned_to, and due_date. Problem and Change extend Task too. We'll mirror that exact real-world relationship with two Script Include classes of our own.

Step one: the base class, TaskUtils. Initialize sets msPerDay once, for later date math. GetOverdueDays reads due_date off any task-like record, computes the difference in milliseconds between right now and that due date using GlideDateTime's getNumericValue method, and converts the result into whole overdue days, returning zero if the date hasn't passed yet. Since due_date genuinely belongs to Task itself, this logic correctly lives here, in the general class, rather than buried inside incident-only code where Problem and Change could never reuse it.

Step two: IncidentUtils extends TaskUtils using Object.extendsObject. Its own initialize calls TaskUtils.prototype.initialize.call this first, so msPerDay is guaranteed to already exist before anything else runs, and only then sets its own majorPriority and majorImpact properties. IsMajorIncident checks a record's priority and impact fields against those two thresholds — logic that only ever makes sense for an incident specifically, which is exactly why it lives in the child class and not the shared parent.

Step three: wiring the finished classes into a real Business Rule on the Incident table. One single new IncidentUtils call gives access to both getOverdueDays, inherited straight from TaskUtils with zero extra code, and isMajorIncident, defined locally on IncidentUtils itself — the two are called side by side to decide whether to add a work note flagging an overdue major incident for someone to notice.

This is the IS-A test from Lesson 13, proven out in an actual build rather than just described. General logic — the overdue-day math — stays on the general class where every task-like record can reach it. Incident-only logic stays on the incident class where it belongs. And if a future developer ever builds a ProblemUtils extending the same TaskUtils, they get fully working overdue-day logic for free, with zero rewriting and zero risk of the two copies drifting apart.

That closes out Chapter 3 on Script Includes — lazy loading, the real class pattern, real inheritance, and now a complete worked build tying all three together. Next, Chapter 4 opens with Lesson 15: UI Policies from a developer's view, moving from server-side classes like these into actual form behavior.
